trees.story:
This cedar started out as stock in a nursery that once covered this corner of Flushing. The parks department's Great Trees entry says it began life in the nursery of Samuel B. Parsons, whose grounds ran through the area, and the park around it takes its name from another tree, a weeping beech.

The cedar is the less famous neighbour and the stranger shape. The register gives it a height of only 12.7 metres but a crown spreading 59 feet, about 18 metres, so it is far wider than it is tall, the flat-topped, layered build of a cedar of Lebanon that has had room to spread. Its trunk measured 59 inches across, about 4.7 metres round, when the city named it a Great Tree in 1985. That figure is four decades old, and the tree has kept the title through the 2024 revision of the list.

Cedar of Lebanon comes from the mountains of the eastern Mediterranean, the tree of the Lebanese flag. That one should have reached Queens through a nineteenth-century nursery catalogue is very much the Parsons story, a family that sold exotic trees to the gardens of a growing country.

It stands in the middle of the park, near the public restroom, about 50 metres from the weeping beech, so the two make one stop. The park is free and open daily. Nobody has published when it was planted. If you know, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its flat, layered crown, about 18 metres across on a tree under 13 metres tall. It stands in the middle of the park near the public restroom, about 50 metres from the weeping beech.

trees.name: The Fused Basswood of Fort Totten

location.address: Fort Totten Park, Underhill Rd and Officers Dr, Bayside

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 2024)

trees.access: Free, public park (Fort Totten Park); the former army post is open to walkers
trees.transport: Bayside station (LIRR) about 2.7 km; local bus to Fort Totten
trees.story: Measured across the trunk, this basswood at Fort Totten comes out at 99 inches, close to the width of a single garage door. That number needs an asterisk, and NYC Parks gives it one. The tree is not one stem but several that grew side by side and fused together long ago, so the 99 inches is the width of a fused mass rather than a single trunk. Round, that works out at about 7.9 metres of wood at chest height, and a shape you will not mistake for anything else in the park. It is also a reminder that the biggest number on a list is not always the oldest tree. A fused basswood can carry a girth that a single trunk of the same age never would, and the honest reading of this one is a big, strange, many-stemmed tree of unknown age. Parks added it to the Great Trees list in 2024, when the city relaunched its roll of remarkable trees. It stands at the corner of Underhill Road and Officers Drive, on the grounds of Fort Totten in Bayside, a former army post that is now a public park open to walkers. Somebody has seen it recently. An iNaturalist record from July 2025 sits near the Parks point. Nobody has recorded when the stems first came up or when they joined. If you know the tree's history, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, several stems fused into one mass about 99 inches across. It stands at the corner of Underhill Road and Officers Drive in Fort Totten Park.

trees.name: The London Plane of Alice Austen Park

location.address: Alice Austen Park, meadow south of the Alice Austen House, Rosebank

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 1985)

trees.access: Alice Austen Park is a public city park, free and open daily. The Alice Austen House museum next to it is open Wednesday to Friday noon to 4pm and Saturday 11am to 4pm, closed Sunday to Tuesday; donations welcome.
trees.transport: Staten Island Railway Clifton station, about 0.6 km; or S51/S78 bus on Bay St (check route)
trees.story: Lightning has hit this plane tree and left its mark, and it is still standing in the meadow south of the Alice Austen House. NYC Parks records the scar on its Great Trees entry, along with the detail that the tree is alive in spite of it. Parks also gives it a starting point. It is believed to have been growing here around 1840, when John Austen, Alice Austen's grandfather, bought the house and set about expanding it. Believed is Parks' word, with no planting record behind it, so read 1840 as a family-era tradition rather than a date. If it holds, the tree is more than 185 years old. The measurements are from the 1985 survey that first put it on the list. The trunk was 54 inches across, about 4.3 metres round, with a crown spreading almost 60 feet over the meadow, though at about 19 metres tall it is broad rather than towering. An iNaturalist record from July 2026 places it alive. Alice Austen Park is open daily and free. The house museum has its own hours and asks a suggested donation, but the tree stands outside it, in the meadow south of the house in Rosebank, on the Staten Island shore. Von Briesen Park, with its own Great Tree, is close by along the same shore. If you know more about when it was planted, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the wide crown, spreading almost 60 feet on a trunk 54 inches across, and its lightning scar. It stands in the meadow south of the Alice Austen House in Alice Austen Park, Rosebank.

trees.name: The Princess Tree of Snug Harbor

location.address: Snug Harbor Cultural Center, west side of the Veterans Memorial Hall Playhouse, Chapel Road, 1000 Richmond Terrace (Parks lists 914)

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 1985)

trees.access: Grounds free, open dawn to dusk seven days a week (Snug Harbor official material via search; some buildings and the Chinese Scholar's Garden take a small fee)
trees.transport: Staten Island Ferry to St George, then S40 bus to Snug Harbor (route unchecked this pass)
trees.story: When NYC Parks measured this tree for its first Great Trees list in 1985, the trunk came out at 65 inches across, about 5.2 metres round. It is a royal paulownia, the tree also called princess tree or empress tree, and it stands on the grounds of Snug Harbor on Staten Island, on the west side of the Veterans Memorial Hall Playhouse off Chapel Road. Parks notes two things that make it easy to pick out. The leaves can grow up to a foot across, big enough to look like a mistake, and in spring the tree carries purple trumpet-shaped flowers. Parks put its height at about 20 metres, so the trunk is the surprise rather than the crown. Snug Harbor is a cultural centre now, and its grounds are free to walk, open from dawn to dusk every day; a few buildings and the Chinese Scholar's Garden charge a small fee, but the paulownia is outside them. One honest caveat about the address. Parks lists the tree at 914 Richmond Terrace and Snug Harbor gives its own address as 1000, but both point to the same campus, and the playhouse is the landmark that matters. The measurements are forty years old. If you have seen it lately or know when it went in, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, up to a foot across, and in spring by purple trumpet flowers. It stands on the west side of the Veterans Memorial Hall Playhouse at Snug Harbor, off Chapel Road.

trees.name: The Cedar of Lebanon of the Olmsted-Beil House

location.address: Olmsted-Beil House Park, 4515 Hylan Boulevard, Great Kills area

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 1985)

trees.access: Free public park around the house; Parks lists it as a city park
trees.transport: Eltingville SIR station about 1.2 km; S55/S59 buses on Hylan Blvd (unchecked)
trees.story: This cedar of Lebanon grows on the farm where Frederick Law Olmsted worked the land for seven years before he designed Central Park. Olmsted farmed here, on Staten Island, from 1848 to 1855, and NYC Parks counts the cedar as one of the trees still remaining from that farm. Parks stops short of saying who planted it or when, so we do too. It is tempting to credit Olmsted with it, and the honest answer is that nobody has. What Parks does give is a location so exact you could use it as directions. The tree stands 35 feet off the left front corner of the house and three feet off the driveway. It measures 46 inches across the trunk, about 3.7 metres round, stands about 82 feet tall and spreads its crown about 40 feet. It has been on the Great Trees list since 1985, the city's roll of its most remarkable trees, and an iNaturalist record from May 2024 places it alive. A black walnut that Parks says Olmsted planted stands about 25 metres away, so see both. The park around the house is free. Nobody has dated the cedar. If you know when it went in, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the position, 35 feet off the left front corner of the house and three feet off the driveway. It stands at Olmsted-Beil House Park, 4515 Hylan Boulevard, about 25 metres from the black walnut.

trees.name: The Black Walnut Olmsted Planted

location.address: Olmsted-Beil House Park, east of the house, 4515 Hylan Boulevard

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 2024)

trees.access: Free public park around the house
trees.transport: Eltingville SIR station about 1.2 km (unchecked bus routes)
trees.story: Before Frederick Law Olmsted designed Central Park, he was a farmer on Staten Island, and NYC Parks says he planted this black walnut himself. Olmsted lived in the house on Hylan Boulevard from 1848 to 1855, and Parks, naming the tree a Great Tree in 2024, credits him with this one and says many of the trees on the property went in around 1850. That makes it, if Parks is right, a tree put in the ground by the man who went on to design Central Park. Take it as Parks' claim. It is the only source we have, and we have found no letter or planting record to back it, so we state it as theirs rather than as settled fact. The tree itself makes a quieter case. Its trunk measures 52 inches across, about 4.2 metres round, which is a big black walnut by any measure. It stands east of the house, about 25 metres from a cedar of Lebanon that Parks also counts among the trees left from Olmsted's farm, so the two make a single stop. The house sits in Olmsted-Beil House Park, a free public park in the Great Kills area. Nobody has measured its age directly. If you know more about what Olmsted planted here, or have seen his own notes on it, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 52 inches across, the big walnut on the east side of the house. It stands in Olmsted-Beil House Park, 4515 Hylan Boulevard, about 25 metres from the cedar of Lebanon.

trees.name: The American Sycamore of Conference House Park

location.address: Conference House Park, behind the Conference House, Tottenville

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 1985)

trees.access: Conference House Park free, open daily; the house museum charges a small fee in season
trees.transport: Tottenville SIR station about 1.1 km on foot
trees.story: The house in front of this sycamore hosted a peace conference in 1776. It is the Conference House in Tottenville, on Staten Island, and NYC Parks puts this American sycamore directly behind it. Do not read that as a witness claim. Parks gives no planting date, and nothing says the tree was here for the conference. The house is the history and the tree is its neighbour today. What the register does give is size. When the tree was first listed as a Great Tree in 1985, it measured 65 inches across the trunk, about 5.2 metres round, and 89 feet tall, with a crown spreading 55 feet. Those are the figures of a tree that has had plenty of room, out on open parkland at the back of a historic house rather than on a crowded street. The tree is still there. An iNaturalist record from September 2026 sits near the Parks point, and the city keeps it in its forestry inventory. Conference House Park is free and open daily; the house museum charges a small fee in season, but the sycamore stands outside it on public parkland. Nobody has dated it. If you know when it went in, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 65 inches across, and its crown spreading about 55 feet. It stands directly behind the Conference House in Conference House Park, Tottenville.

trees.name: The Multi-Trunk English Elm of the West Drive

location.address: Prospect Park, west drive between the Garfield Entrance and Meadowport Arch

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees of New York City (designated 1985)

trees.access: Free, public park, open daily
trees.transport: Grand Army Plaza station (2, 3), about 0.5 km on foot
trees.story: NYC Parks keeps this elm on its Great Trees list partly as a lesson in shape. The native American elm grows in the shape of a vase. This is an English elm, an introduced tree, and it does something else entirely. It rises on several trunks at once, and Parks chose it in 1985 to show the difference. The size is real but needs one caveat. Parks measured it at 74 inches across, about 5.9 metres round, which would make it a giant among elms, but that figure is taken across a mass of several stems rather than one trunk, so do not compare it with a single-stemmed tree. The other numbers need no caveat. It stood 96 feet tall at that survey, about 29 metres, with a crown spreading 66 feet over the West Drive, and it is still there; an iNaturalist record from May 2026 sits near the Parks point. It stands on Prospect Park's West Drive, between the Garfield entrance and Meadowport Arch, on free public parkland open daily. The Camperdown Elm near the Boathouse is in the same park for a second stop. Nobody has dated this one. If you know when it went in, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its several trunks rising together, unlike the single vase-shaped stem of an American elm. It stands beside Prospect Park's West Drive, between the Garfield entrance and Meadowport Arch.

trees.name: The English Elm of Stuyvesant Square

location.address: Western gate of Stuyvesant Square Park, Second Avenue side

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees

trees.access: Free; public park, open daily.
trees.transport: L train to First Avenue or 6 to Astor Place, about 10 minutes' walk; check route (not verified).
trees.story: This elm may be older than the park it stands in. NYC Parks thinks it was already growing here before 1836, the year Peter Gerard Stuyvesant gave this land to the city. Thought to, not known to. There is no planting record, and the claim is the register's own careful wording. If it holds, the tree was here first and the square came to it. Then there is the height. Parks measured it at 108.2 feet, about 33 metres, a tall tree by any standard and a striking one to find on a square in Manhattan. The trunk is slimmer than the height suggests, 42 inches across in the 1985 survey that first put it on the Great Trees list and 44 in the city's current forestry inventory, about 3.4 metres round. That inventory files it under Ulmus minor 'Atinia', the botanist's name for the English elm, and found it in Good condition in February 2026. For a tree that may have been standing here for close to two centuries, that is a decent report. It stands just inside the western gate, on the Second Avenue side of the square, free to visit whenever the park is open. If you know more about how old it really is, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, about 33 metres, on a trunk only 42 to 44 inches across. It stands just inside the western gate of Stuyvesant Square, on the Second Avenue side.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of Isham Park

location.address: Isham Park, southeast corner at Broadway and West 211th Street

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees

trees.access: Free; public park.
trees.transport: 1 to 215th Street or A to Inwood-207th Street, a few minutes' walk; check route (not verified).
trees.verify_notes: Parks (1985): one of the best-known trees in the neighbourhood; 58 in diameter, 71.3 ft. Tree Map ID 5096375: forestry point dbh 58, Excellent, coordinates match. Pin confirmed by register tree-point.
trees.story:
The parks department calls this ginkgo one of the best-known trees in its neighbourhood. It stands at the south-east corner of Isham Park, where Broadway meets West 211th Street, on a trunk 58 inches across, about 4.6 metres round, and about 22 metres tall. The city named it a Great Tree in 1985, and four decades later its forestry inventory records the same 58 inches and rates the tree excellent, the top grade it gives.

Ginkgo is the last survivor of a group of trees that was widespread when dinosaurs were alive, and it reached America only in the 1780s, as a garden curiosity in Philadelphia. Since then New Yorkers have planted it by the thousand, because it shrugs off salt, smog and compacted soil. Most of those street ginkgos are young and slim. This one shows what the species does when it is left alone in a park for a long time.

Isham Park was once part of the Isham family's estate in Inwood, given to the city in the early twentieth century. The ginkgo now holds its busiest corner, beside the traffic of Broadway, a few minutes' walk from the 1 train at 215th Street and the A at Inwood-207th Street.

Nobody has published when it was planted, or whether it went in before or after the land became a park. If you know, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its fan-shaped leaves, which turn butter yellow in autumn, on a trunk about 4.6 metres round. It stands at the south-east corner of Isham Park, at Broadway and West 211th Street.

best_time.label: November, when the fan-shaped leaves turn butter yellow and drop almost together

trees.name: The Plane Tree of King's Bridge

location.address: East side of Corlear Avenue just south of West 231st Street

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees

trees.access: Free; street tree on Corlear Avenue.
trees.transport: 1 train to 231st Street, then a walk toward Corlear Avenue; check route (not verified).
trees.story: Close to this street corner in the Bronx, Washington's army crossed a bridge in retreat. NYC Parks puts the tree near the site of the King's Bridge, built by Frederick Philipse in 1693, and says that Washington's troops crossed it falling back after the loss of Fort Washington on 16 November 1776. The bridge is the history here; the tree is what still stands near where it was. Even the name of the tree is a small argument. Parks listed it in 1985 as an American sycamore. The city's own forestry inventory, which carries the same coordinates and the same 54 inch trunk, records it as a London plane, the hybrid of the American sycamore and the Oriental plane. We follow the inventory, and the two are close enough kin that a reader standing underneath may want to judge for themselves. Either way it is a big tree for a side street. The trunk is 54 inches across, about 4.3 metres round, and Parks measured it at 98.4 feet tall, about 30 metres. The inventory found it in Good condition in January 2024. It stands on the east side of Corlear Avenue just south of West 231st Street, a public street tree you can walk up to at any hour. Nobody has dated it. If you know when it went in, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 54 inches across, and the height, about 30 metres. It stands on the east side of Corlear Avenue just south of West 231st Street.

trees.name: The White Oak of the Property Line

location.address: Van Cortlandt Park, north side of Gun Hill Road at Mosholu Parkway North

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees

trees.access: Free; park edge on Gun Hill Road opposite the Mosholu Teaching Forest.
trees.transport: 4 train to Mosholu Parkway, a walk; check route (not verified).
trees.story: Somebody may once have planted this white oak to mark where their land ended. That is what NYC Parks believes, saying it went in hundreds of years ago as a property-line marker, though Parks gives no date, no names and no deed, so take the hundreds of years as a belief rather than a measurement. Nobody has recorded whose boundary it was. The tree outlasted the line. Its trunk now measures 58 inches across, about 4.6 metres round, on the north side of Gun Hill Road at Mosholu Parkway North, where Van Cortlandt Park meets the traffic. It joined the Great Trees list in 2024, the city's roll of its most remarkable trees, and its route there is a story of its own. It was not put forward by a forester or a historian but by an artist-in-residence working with the NYC Urban Field Station. An artist picked this one out of a park full of trees. The city's forestry inventory last recorded it in April 2023 and called it Good, with coordinates that match the Parks listing. It stands at the park's edge across Gun Hill Road from the Mosholu Teaching Forest, so it is easy to reach on foot and free at any hour, no trail walking needed. Nobody has dated it. If you know anything about the old line it marked, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 58 inches across, at the very edge of the park beside the road. It stands on the north side of Gun Hill Road at Mosholu Parkway North, opposite the Mosholu Teaching Forest.

trees.name: The Circus Ground Oak of Saratoga Park

location.address: Saratoga Park, south side of the path north of the children's playground

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees

trees.access: Free; public park.
trees.transport: A or C to Utica Avenue, or J to Chauncey Street, a walk; check route (not verified).
trees.story: Before Saratoga Park was a park, the whole block was a circus ground, and NYC Parks thinks this red oak likely dates from those days. Likely is their word, and it is worth keeping. There is no planting record and no ring count, only a tree big enough to make the idea plausible and a block with a history odd enough to make it memorable. The more recent history is better documented. When the park was renovated in 2023, the new playground was laid out around a central corridor to protect the tree, so the design bends to the oak rather than the other way round. In 2024 Parks added it to its Great Trees list, the city's roll of its most remarkable trees. The trunk measures 54 inches across, about 4.3 metres round, and the city's forestry inventory found it in Good condition in December 2025. It stands on the south side of the path just north of the children's playground, a public park tree you can walk right up to. If you know when it was planted, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 54 inches across, the big oak the playground was laid out around. It stands on the south side of the path just north of the children's playground in Saratoga Park.

trees.name: The Oak Moved from Prospect Park

location.address: 195 East 3rd Street

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees

trees.access: Free; Parks-inventoried street tree in front of a house, seen from the sidewalk.
trees.transport: F or G to Ditmas Avenue or Fort Hamilton Parkway, a walk; check route (not verified).
trees.verify_notes: Parks (2024): per the nominator and family legend, a former Parks worker took a small oak sapling from Prospect Park and planted it here in 1958 (legend, one family source); 50 in diameter, the largest tree for many blocks. Age derived from that 1958 planting story. Tree Map ID 1242920: Good, updated 2026-07-31, coordinates match. Pin confirmed by register tree-point. Earlier lead worried it stands in front of a home; the inventory records it as a Parks street tree.
trees.story:
A former parks worker, the family story goes, walked out of Prospect Park in 1958 with a small oak sapling and planted it on East 3rd Street in Kensington. Today that northern red oak has a trunk 50 inches across, about four metres round, and the parks department, adding it to its Great Trees list in 2024, called it the largest tree for many blocks.

The story is a legend in the honest sense. It comes from the nominator and the family, one source, and nobody has a receipt for the sapling. But the tree fits it. A red oak planted in 1958 would be about seventy now, somewhere between 65 and 75 if the year is a little off, and red oak is among the faster-growing oaks of the eastern forest, so a trunk this thick in that time is plausible rather than miraculous.

If the legend holds, this is a piece of Prospect Park that moved a short way south. The park was laid out by Olmsted and Vaux in the 1860s, and one of its seedlings now shades a residential block instead, bigger than anything else on the street.

It stands in front of 195 East 3rd Street, and the city's forestry inventory records it as a street tree in good condition, last updated in July 2026. It is in front of somebody's house, so look from the sidewalk and let the house be. If you know more of the family story, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the largest tree for many blocks, a northern red oak about four metres round at chest height. It stands on the sidewalk in front of 195 East 3rd Street.

trees.name: The Phoenix Ginkgo

location.address: Green-Wood Cemetery, Brooklyn (Celebrated Tree Walk stop, near the Brown family mausoleum)

trees.access: Free; Green-Wood is open daily (hours at green-wood.com/hours); the Celebrated Trees Walk is on the cemetery's own visitor map
trees.transport: Check route: Green-Wood main entrance at Fifth Ave and 25th St; Sunset Park entrance at 36th St (subway lines and walk times not checked).
trees.story: Twelve ginkgo trees came up from one stump here, and over the years they have grown together into a single tree. Green-Wood Cemetery calls it the Phoenix Ginkgo, and the name does the explaining. Something cut or killed the original tree down to its stump, the stump refused to quit, and the twelve shoots that rose from it have since inosculated, the botanist's word for stems that touch, graft and fuse into one living body. What happened to the first tree, the cemetery does not say, and we will not guess. The story here is the comeback, not the cause. Green-Wood is an accredited arboretum as well as a burial ground, and it puts this tree on its Celebrated Trees walk, printed on its own visitor map in 2023 and again in 2025, near the Brown family mausoleum. Nobody has published a girth or an age, and a tape measure would struggle to say where one stem ends and the next begins. Come in November if you can. Ginkgos turn butter yellow in late autumn and drop their leaves within a day or two, and a dozen fused trunks turning at once is worth the timing. The cemetery is free to enter and open daily, with the hours on its website, and the Celebrated Trees walk is marked on the cemetery's visitor map. If you know when the original tree came down, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the many ginkgo stems, about a dozen, fused together into one tree. It stands on Green-Wood Cemetery's Celebrated Trees walk, near the Brown family mausoleum.

best_time.label: November, when the fused crown turns butter gold

trees.name: The Weeping Beech Tunnel at Green-Wood

location.address: Green-Wood Cemetery, Brooklyn (over Larch Avenue, Celebrated Tree Walk stop)

trees.access: Free; Green-Wood is open daily (hours at green-wood.com/hours); the tunnel is on a cemetery drive and path stop of the owner's Celebrated Trees Walk
trees.transport: Check route: Green-Wood main entrance at Fifth Ave and 25th St; Sunset Park entrance at 36th St (subway lines and walk times not checked)

location_site.name: Weeping beech tunnel on Larch Avenue, Green-Wood

trees.verify_notes: Green-Wood's own visitor map (2023 and 2025 editions) lists 'Weeping Beech Tunnel' as a group of six weeping European beeches whose cascading canopies form a tunnel, a visitor favourite. A Green-Wood tree blog (2009, a blog, a finding aid only) says the most enchanting weeping beech hangs over Larch Avenue and that you must walk or drive under the canopy to go up the road. One compact ensemble with one place to stand (the road under the canopy). Pin: OSM natural=tree node 12609928197 'Weeping Beech' (one point for six trees, so approximate, with a 50 m site). A Brooklyn guide calls it elms; the owner's map and the blog say beech, the owner wins. No planting date, girth or age in any source. Not checked: that the OSM node sits exactly on Larch Avenue (road geometry fetch failed, Overpass at capacity). What tells it apart: the canopy closes over the road.
trees.story:
At Green-Wood the road goes under the trees, not past them. Six weeping European beeches stand together over Larch Avenue, and their branches hang down and meet until the drive runs through a tunnel of leaves. The cemetery's own visitor map lists the Weeping Beech Tunnel as a stop on its Celebrated Trees Walk and calls it a visitor favourite. A Green-Wood tree blog put it more plainly in 2009, saying you have to walk or drive under the canopy to go up the road at all.

Weeping beeches grow their limbs outward and then down, so an old one becomes a room with walls of foliage. Six together over a road make a corridor. One Brooklyn guide calls them elms; the cemetery's map and its tree blog both say beech, and the owner of the ground gets the last word.

Green-Wood opened in 1838 and soon became one of the most visited places in America, with crowds coming to picnic among the graves before New York had Central Park. Its 478 acres hold Leonard Bernstein, Jean-Michel Basquiat and Boss Tweed. Entry is free and the gates open daily.

No source gives a planting date, a girth or an age for these beeches, and nobody has said whether all six went in together. If you know, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the road itself, which runs under a closed canopy of six weeping beeches whose branches hang down and meet overhead. It stands on Larch Avenue, a stop on the cemetery's Celebrated Trees Walk.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the hanging leaves over the road turn gold and copper

trees.name: The Blue Atlas Cedars of Queens Botanical Garden

location.address: Queens Botanical Garden, 43-50 Main Street, Flushing, Queens (Main Street entrance, either side of the tree gate sculpture)

trees.access: Garden entry is ticketed or free on some days; check queensbotanical.org for hours and prices before going. The cedars stand at the Main Street entrance (stop #1 on the garden map)
trees.transport: Check route: the 7 train terminates at Flushing-Main St, near the garden (walk time not checked)
trees.verify_notes: The garden's own visitor guide (2016 PDF) says two blue atlas cedars that frame the iconic tree gate sculpture at the Main Street entrance (#1 on the map) are original plantings taken from the 1939 World's Fair 'Gardens on Parade' site, when the garden moved to Main Street in 1961 (Wikipedia gives the move as completed with dedication 19 Oct 1963 and says THREE cedars were transplanted; the owner says two: conflict, kept both counts). Age derived from a documented specimen history: planted for the 1939 fair, so at least 85 years in the ground, possibly older nursery stock; broad range given, no girth recorded. Pin: garden coordinate from Wikipedia (40.7504, -73.8288); the entrance itself was not pinned (Nominatim and Overpass gave no entrance node), so the walker finds it by the tree gate sculpture, not by the coordinate. The garden is a walk-through garden, not a small site, so no location_site. Alive: no dated record of these cedars specifically; the 2016 guide is the latest owner statement, lifecheck RECENT only for the garden area (iNaturalist 2026-10-15). Flagged.
trees.story:
These cedars were exhibits at the 1939 World's Fair. They were planted for Gardens on Parade, the fair's horticultural show in Flushing Meadows, and when Queens Botanical Garden, which grew out of that exhibit, moved to its present ground on Main Street, the cedars moved with it. The garden's own visitor guide calls them original plantings from the fair site. That puts them at least 85 years in the ground, and possibly older, since nobody recorded how old the nursery stock was in 1939.

How many came is a small mystery. The garden's guide says two, and two now frame the tree gate sculpture at the Main Street entrance. Wikipedia says three cedars were transplanted. The sources also differ on timing, the guide placing the move in 1961 and Wikipedia giving the new garden's dedication as 19 October 1963. Either way, moving a conifer of that size is a serious job, and these survived it.

The tree is the North African Atlas cedar in its blue-needled form, Glauca, which turns a whole crown silver-blue. The colour holds all year, so there is no wrong season to visit.

You meet them before anything else, since they are stop number one on the garden map. Entry is ticketed on some days and free on others, so check queensbotanical.org before you go. Nobody has published a girth for either tree. If you have measured one, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by their silver-blue needles and by where they stand, one either side of the tree gate sculpture at the Main Street entrance, stop number one on the garden map.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of John Golden Park

location.address: John Golden Park (Crocheron Park area), Bayside

trees.story:
Boss Tweed is said to have hidden from the law near this ginkgo. NYC Parks links the tree to William M. Tweed, who escaped from Ludlow Street Jail and, by the account on its Great Trees entry, lay low at the Crocheron family house that once stood on this ground. The city later bought the property, and the land is now John Golden Park. The Tweed story is Parks' telling and we have found it nowhere else, so treat it as local lore rather than a court record.

The tree itself needs no legend. It is about 25 metres tall, with a trunk 37 inches across, close to three metres round, and a crown about 33 feet wide. It went on the Great Trees list in the city's first survey, in 1985, and an iNaturalist record from July 2026 shows it still standing. Nobody has published when it was planted, so its age stays open. If you know, tell us.

It stands behind the baseball fields, near the public restroom, in a free park in Bayside that is open every day. Bayside station on the Long Island Rail Road's Port Washington branch is about 1.3 kilometres away on foot. Come in November, when a ginkgo turns butter yellow.

trees.name: The Swamp White Oak of Bowne Park

location.address: Bowne Park, between the northwest entrance and the pond, Flushing

trees.story:
NYC Parks did not hedge on this one. When the swamp white oak in Bowne Park joined the Great Trees list in 2024, the citation called it an exceptionally large tree for its kind and the most impressive tree in the park. The trunk is 50 inches across, close to four metres round, a serious waistline for an oak named after wet ground and here growing in a neighbourhood park in Queens.

The 2024 listing came out of the city's Great Tree Search, nearly four decades after the first list of 1985, and it put this oak among the newest names on the roll. Parks gives its Tree Map number, 5085084, so you can find the same trunk in the city's forestry inventory, and an iNaturalist record from August 2025 shows it still standing.

What nobody has published is its age. Nothing we have read dates this tree, and we will not guess from the size of the trunk. If you know when it went in, or what the ground looked like before the park, tell us.

It stands between the northwest entrance and the pond, in a free park open daily. Flushing-Main Street, the end of the 7 train and a Long Island Rail Road stop, is about 2.3 kilometres away, with local buses from Main Street.

trees.name: The Willow Oak of Steinway Street

location.address: 23-24 Steinway Street, Astoria

trees.story:
This oak waves at trains. That is NYC Parks' own phrase for the willow oak outside 23-24 Steinway Street, whose branches reach toward the trains crossing the Hell Gate Bridge, and it is a fair description of a street tree that has grown far bigger than the sidewalk it was given.

The trunk is 42 inches across, about 3.4 metres round. Parks called it extremely large when it joined the Great Trees list in 2024, and it earned that on what Parks describes as a busy commercial and residential stretch of Astoria. Most of the city's great trees have a park around them. This one has a sidewalk and the traffic of Steinway Street.

A willow oak is easy to mistake for something else. The leaves are narrow and pointed, more like a willow's than an oak's, and only the acorns give it away. Nobody has published when this one was planted, so its age stays open. If you know, tell us.

An iNaturalist record from September 2026 shows it standing. It is on the public sidewalk, so you can see it at any hour. The Astoria Boulevard station on the N and W lines is about 800 metres away on foot.

trees.name: The River Birch of Corporal Kennedy Street

location.address: 35-26 Corporal Kennedy Street, Bayside

trees.story:
A river birch this size is unusual anywhere, and NYC Parks found one growing out of a Bayside sidewalk. The tree outside 35-26 Corporal Kennedy Street has several stems that together measure 57 inches across, about 4.5 metres round, and a canopy that arches clear over the street. Parks put it on the Great Trees list in 2024 and named exactly that as the reason, a very large multi-stemmed river birch, uncommon at this size and more uncommon still as a street tree.

The number needs one caution. A multi-stemmed tree is measured across its stems, so 57 inches is the mass of several trunks rising from one base, not a single column of wood. That is also what you see standing under it, a cluster rather than a pillar.

Nobody has published its age. The latest sighting we found is an iNaturalist record from August 2024, recent enough to trust but not as fresh as we would like. If you pass it and it is still there, or if you know when it was planted, tell us.

It stands on the public sidewalk, so it can be seen at any time. Bayside station on the Long Island Rail Road is about 500 metres away on foot, and the ginkgo of John Golden Park, another Great Tree, is about a kilometre to the north.

trees.name: The Willow Oak of Clove Lake

location.address: Clove Lakes Park, shore of Clove Lake, 150 ft north of Victory Blvd near the basketball courts

trees.story:
NYC Parks listed this tree as half of a pair. On the shore of Clove Lake, about 150 feet north of Victory Boulevard, two willow oaks share a single entry on the Great Trees list, which they have held since the city's first survey in 1985. The entry gives one set of measurements for the pair, a trunk 43 inches across, about 3.4 metres round, close to 26 metres of height and a crown spreading some 43 feet at the water's edge.

The name tells you what to look for. A willow oak has narrow leaves that read as willow from a distance, which is a neat trick for a tree standing beside a lake where you would expect real willows. Up close the acorns settle it.

Nobody has published when the pair went in, so the age stays open. If you know, tell us. An iNaturalist record from September 2026 shows them still standing.

Clove Lakes Park is free and open daily, and the walk is the reason to come. The Clove Lakes Colossus, a tulip tree and Staten Island's tallest, stands about 1.3 kilometres away at the north end of the same park, so the two make one lake walk. The oaks are by the basketball courts near Victory Boulevard, reached by bus from St George.

trees.name: The Pagoda Tree of Von Briesen Park

location.address: Von Briesen Park, southern end where the path curves east-west, Rosebank

trees.story:
The man who founded the Legal Aid Society may have known this tree. NYC Parks believes the Japanese pagoda tree at the southern end of Von Briesen Park was part of the original estate of Arthur Von Briesen, whose heirs gave the land to the city in 1945. Believed is Parks' word, and no planting record has surfaced to firm it up, so read the estate link as likely rather than proven.

What is not in doubt is its size. The trunk is 48 inches across, about 3.8 metres round, and Parks called it unusually large for its species when it named the tree a Great Tree in 2024. An iNaturalist record from August 2026 shows it still standing.

It also blooms late, which is its best trick. In late summer, when most trees have long finished, it hangs out pendant sprays of flowers. Nobody has published its age. If you know when it was planted, tell us.

Find it where the path curves from east to west at the south end of the park, which is free and open daily. Clifton station on the Staten Island Railway is about 900 metres away, and the plane tree of Alice Austen Park is about 1.3 kilometres along the same shore, so the two make one walk.

trees.name: The White Pine of Blue Heron Park

location.address: Blue Heron Park Preserve, just southeast of the Blue Heron Nature Center

trees.story:
This is the last of its kind in Blue Heron Park. NYC Parks says the eastern white pine just southeast of the Blue Heron Nature Center is the only white pine of this size left in the preserve, and it chose the tree for the Great Trees list in 2024 for its age rather than its bulk.

That choice shows in the numbers. The trunk is 27 inches across, about 2.2 metres round, slim beside the oaks and planes on the rest of the city's list. The height is another matter. Parks gives it about 90 feet, close to 27 metres, and a white pine puts that height into one straight stem, so this tree reads as a mast rather than a crown.

Parks does not say how old it is, only that age was the reason it was picked, and nobody else has published a figure. We will not invent one from the trunk. If you know its story, or when the pines around it went, tell us.

Blue Heron Park Preserve is free and open daily, in Annadale on the South Shore of Staten Island. Start at the nature center and look southeast. The Annadale station on the Staten Island Railway is roughly a kilometre away. An iNaturalist record from October 2026 shows the pine still standing.

trees.name: The Catalpa of Historic Richmond Town

location.address: Historic Richmond Town, behind the tin shop, 441 Clarke Avenue (Parks lists LaTourette Park)

trees.story:
Behind a tin shop in New York City's only historic village restoration stands a catalpa with a trunk 47 inches across. That is about 3.75 metres round, and it is why NYC Parks named this tree to the Great Trees list in 2024. The citation is short. Parks chose it for its large size and left the rest to the setting.

The setting is Historic Richmond Town, founded in 1939 by the Staten Island Historical Society. It now covers more than 100 acres and over two dozen buildings dating from the 17th century to the 20th, so the tree keeps company with buildings from four centuries of Staten Island life. Parks files it under neighbouring LaTourette Park, but it is the village you walk through to reach it.

Parks names only the genus, catalpa, and not the species. If you can tell from the leaves or the long seed pods, tell us. Nobody has published its age either, and the village's founding date says nothing about when the tree went in.

Entry to the village needs a ticket, and by most accounts it opens from Wednesday to Sunday, so check historicrichmondtown.org for hours and prices before you go. The address is 441 Clarke Avenue, with buses from St George.

trees.name: The American Elm of Sunset Park

location.address: Sunset Park, top of the hill in the central lawn

trees.story:
This elm was the face of the hunt before it was a winner. When NYC Parks ran its Great Tree Search in 2023, asking New Yorkers to put forward the city's best trees, the advertising photo was the silhouette of this American elm on the hill in Sunset Park. A year later Parks put it on the Great Trees list itself.

It earned the picture on shape more than size. The trunk is 38 inches across, about three metres round, respectable rather than record-breaking. What Parks chose to show was the outline of the tree against the sky at the top of the central lawn, and an American elm's crown is the kind of outline that sells a campaign. The species was hit hard across the Northeast by Dutch elm disease, which makes a healthy one in an open lawn worth the climb.

Nobody has published its age, so we leave it open. If you know when it went in, tell us. An iNaturalist record from September 2025 shows it standing.

Sunset Park is free and open daily, on the Brooklyn slope above the harbour. Walk up to the top of the hill in the central lawn. The 36th Street station on the D, N and R lines is about 900 metres away on foot.

trees.name: The Elm of Amersfort Park

location.address: Amersfort Park, near the Avenue J and East 39th Street entrance, Flatlands

trees.story:
Five feet across is a lot of elm. The American elm near the Avenue J and East 39th Street entrance of Amersfort Park has a trunk 60 inches in diameter, about 4.8 metres round, and NYC Parks added it to the Great Trees list in 2024. Its citation calls it a tall elm and one of many old-growth trees in Amersfort Park, which says something about this small park in Flatlands. Parks picked one trunk, and named the crowd around it in the same breath.

Nobody has published its age, and a wide trunk alone cannot date a tree, so the age stays open. Old growth is Parks' phrase for the park's trees as a group, not a date for this one. If you know when it was planted, tell us.

One honest caution. The most recent sighting we found is an iNaturalist record from September 2023, which is older than we would like for a tree we send people to. Parks still lists it on its Great Trees map. If you visit and it is standing, or if it is not, tell us so we can keep this page right.

The park is free and open daily. There is no subway close by, so take a bus along Avenue J or Flatbush Avenue and walk in from the Avenue J and East 39th Street corner, where the elm stands.

location.address: Marine Park, near Gerritsen Ballfields, southeast of Ball Field 3

trees.name: The Black Oak of Albany Avenue

location.address: 1319 Albany Avenue, East Flatbush

trees.story:
This oak was here before the houses. NYC Parks says the black oak outside 1319 Albany Avenue predates the residential development of East Flatbush, and believes it stands where the Paerdegat Woods once grew. The Brooklyn Paper has reported that those woods were cut in the 1940s. If Parks is right, this street tree is not a street tree at all, but a survivor of a forest that the street replaced.

Believes is the word Parks uses, and we keep it. No survey has tied this trunk to the old woods by date, and the age of the tree has never been published. What can be measured is the trunk, 47 inches across, about 3.75 metres round, and Parks named it a Great Tree in 2024.

It has a partner. About 240 metres east, outside 1281 Troy Avenue, a second black oak with an even wider trunk carries the same story, and Parks lists the two as the remnants of the same woods. Seeing both takes a few minutes on foot.

Both stand on the public sidewalk, so you can see them at any time. Buses run along Albany Avenue. The nearest subway stations, Utica Avenue and Nostrand Avenue, are more than 1.5 kilometres away. If you know how old these oaks are, tell us.

location.address: Crotona Park, near the Claremont Parkway entrance on Crotona Park East, Bronx

trees.story: No other elm in Crotona Park comes close. The city's forestry survey counts this American elm at 52 inches across the trunk, roughly four metres round, and finds no second elm in the park that reaches 50. In 2024 NYC Parks put it on its list of Great Trees, the first time that list had been updated in about forty years, which puts this corner of the Bronx on the city's official roll of its finest trees. The Parks listing places it on the north side, near the entrance where Claremont Parkway meets Crotona Park East. That is about all the official record says. trees.story: This is a willow with a school timetable. Children from the nearby New Amsterdam School climb it, and since 2011 a New School class in community gardening has met beneath it, so this is a working tree rather than an ornament. It grows in El Jardin del Paraiso on East 5th Street, described by the local paper Village View as the neighbourhood's largest community garden, and in 2024 NYC Parks added it to its list of Great Trees. The city's forestry survey puts this one at 41 inches across the trunk, a little over three metres round, which is very large for its kind on a Manhattan block. Village View credits the planting to Liz Christy, years ago, without a year, and no other source we found dates it. So its age stays open. If you were there when it went in, tell us. Two practical notes. The garden is a community garden, not a park, so it opens only at its posted hours; check before you go. And our pin is approximate, since we could not confirm the forestry point sits inside the garden fence. Once you are at the garden gate, though, there is no other willow to mistake it for.

trees.name: The Elms of the Heather Garden Promenade

location.address: Stan Michels Promenade above the Heather Garden, Fort Tryon Park, Manhattan

trees.story: Every other year, someone injects these elms with medicine. The Fort Tryon Park Trust pays to inoculate 48 American elms in the park against Dutch elm disease, because many of the original trees have already died. The survivors on the Stan Michels Promenade are the park's best-known. The Trust describes the park's elms as more than a hundred years old, planted widely in the early 1900s. That is a date for the planting as a whole, not a birth certificate for any one tree, so read it as over a century and probably not by much more. The promenade runs above the Heather Garden, which the Trust gives as opening in 1935, and the elms line it. The one people mention most stands at the northern end, its low branches reaching out over the garden beds. The city's forestry survey finds the two biggest American elms in the park here, 59 and 54 inches across the trunk, about 70 metres apart. The larger works out at nearly five metres round. We cannot yet say which of the two is the northern-end tree, so this entry is the pair, and our pin sits on one of them rather than a proven favourite. Both were logged in full leaf and good condition. Walk the promenade end to end and you have seen both, along with what a century of careful nursing looks like.

trees.name: The Ginkgo of the Cloisters Lawn

location.address: South end of the Cloisters Lawn, Fort Tryon Park, Manhattan

trees.story: The Cloisters charges for entry; the Great Tree on its lawn does not. This ginkgo stands at the south end of the Cloisters Lawn in Fort Tryon Park, and NYC Parks includes it in its 2024 list of Great Trees. Its trunk is around four metres round. The two measurements we have disagree slightly, 48 inches across in the Parks listing and 52 in the city's forestry survey, a gap that ordinary growth between surveys or a different tape position easily explains. Either way it is one of only two ginkgos in the park with a trunk over 20 inches; the other stands about 450 metres south, near the Heather Garden. Nobody has published when this one was planted, so its age is an open question. If you know, tell us. The forestry survey logged it alive and in good condition in February 2025. The lawn is ordinary public park, open to anyone walking through Fort Tryon, and the museum is a separate visit. Our pin sits on the forestry point nearest the lawn, which we think is the Great Tree but have not proven, so it is marked approximate. Come in November, when ginkgos turn gold all at once and then drop their leaves within a day or two.

trees.name: The Pawpaw of the Plant Family Collection

location.address: Brooklyn Botanic Garden, Plant Family Collection between Daffodil Hill and Oak Circle, 990 Washington Ave

trees.story: Its trunk is only ten inches across, and New York has counted it among its Great Trees since 1985. This is a pawpaw, a member of the custard-apple family, and NYC Parks describes its fruit as edible and banana-like and its leaves as large and umbrella-like. A trunk you could nearly close your hands around sits on the same official roll as the city's giant elms and oaks. It stands in the Plant Family Collection of the Brooklyn Botanic Garden, between Daffodil Hill and Oak Circle, about ten metres tall with a crown a little over seven metres wide. The Parks entry gives a planting year of 1923, which makes it roughly a century old. The Parks list page has also carried 1932, and no other source we know of settles it, so treat the century as approximate, give or take a decade. Either date means the tree had already been growing in Brooklyn for half a century or more when the city first drew up its list of Great Trees, and it has stayed on that list for forty years since. Whatever earned it that place, it was not size. Come for a fruit nobody expects in Brooklyn, on a tree that has lasted. Entry to the garden is paid, with free times; check bbg.org before you go. Our pin is approximate, inside the garden, so find the collection first and the tree second.

trees.name: The Chinese Parasol Tree of the Rock Garden

location.address: Brooklyn Botanic Garden, south of the Rock Garden

trees.story: This tree arrived in Brooklyn by government post. In 1971 the US National Arboretum sent it to the Brooklyn Botanic Garden, and fourteen years later, in 1985, it was on the city's first list of Great Trees. Fourteen years from arrival to the city's honour roll is fast going. It is a Chinese parasol tree, Firmiana simplex. NYC Parks records a crown about 25 feet across over a trunk only 12.25 inches thick, and a height of about twelve metres. On a tree this slim, the canopy carries the whole effect. Its age is about as well known as any tree's in the garden, since the arrival is on record, so it is a little over half a century old. Nothing older is being claimed for it, and nothing needs to be. It stands just south of the Rock Garden, which puts it in good company. The Great Tree winterberry grows about 25 metres away, and the garden's Caucasian wingnut, another Great Tree, is in the same corner, so three of the city's listed trees can be seen in a few minutes without retracing your steps. Our pin is approximate, since the register gives coordinates inside the garden but no map id for the tree. Entry to the garden is paid, with some free times; check bbg.org before you go.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by a broad crown, about 25 feet across, on a slim trunk barely a foot thick. It stands just south of the Rock Garden, about 25 metres from the Great Tree winterberry.

trees.name: The Winterberry of the Rock Garden

location.address: Brooklyn Botanic Garden, south side of the Rock Garden

trees.story: When the city measured this holly in 1985, its trunk was 27.5 inches across, about 2.2 metres round. The tree is a mountain winterberry, Ilex montana, a holly, and it has been one of New York's Great Trees since that first list. NYC Parks records it at about 11.7 metres tall with a crown 28 feet wide. It stands on the south side of the Rock Garden at the Brooklyn Botanic Garden. The Parks entry ties the species to the garden's beginning, noting winterberry among the 12,000 plants the garden advertised when it was founded in 1910. Read that carefully. It says the garden had winterberries from the start. It does not say this is one of them, and no source gives this tree a planting date. So its age is open, and if anyone at the garden knows its history, we would like to hear it. The 1985 measurement is the latest the register gives, so the trunk you see today may well be larger. The tree is still on the city's list forty years on. The register pin sits inside the garden without a map id for the individual tree, so ours is approximate. The Chinese parasol tree, also a Great Tree, stands about 25 metres away, and the garden's Caucasian wingnut is in the same corner. Entry is paid, with some free times; check bbg.org.

trees.name: The Parrotia of Kissena Park

location.address: Kissena Park, thirty feet south of the public restroom

trees.story: A tree native to Iran stands thirty feet south of a public restroom in Queens, and the city lists it among its Great Trees. This is a Persian parrotia, a species NYC Parks calls rare, and it grows in Kissena Park in Flushing, about 17 metres tall with a crown some 44 feet across. Parks presents it as a living record of the trees introduced by the nursery of Samuel B. Parsons, and it has been on the city's list of Great Trees since the first one, in 1985. Forty years on that list is a long run for any tree. The trunk is 16 inches across, a little over a metre round, slim beside the giant oaks and elms on the same roll. Look closely at the bark, which Parks describes as brown and flaky, the detail most worth stopping for on a tree whose size will not stop you on its own. Nobody has published a planting date, so we give it no age. If the park's history records when this one went in, or you know more about the Parsons connection, tell us. The directions on the register are refreshingly practical, and they are the best ones we have. Find the restroom and walk thirty feet south. Our pin is approximate, since the register gives no map id for the individual tree. About 90 metres away stands the park's Manchurian linden, another Great Tree, so the two make one short stop.

trees.name: The Riis Beeches of Maple Grove Cemetery

location.address: Maple Grove Cemetery, by the grave of Elizabeth Riis, Kew Gardens

trees.story: Jacob Riis planted these two beeches in 1905, beside the grave of his wife, Elizabeth. That is the whole of the record NYC Parks gives, and it is enough. Two American beeches, standing together at one grave in Maple Grove Cemetery in Kew Gardens, have been growing there for about 120 years, and since 1985 they have been on the city's list of Great Trees, entered as a pair. The planting date comes from that single Parks note. We know of no second source for it, so read 1905 as the city's word rather than a date carved anywhere. When Parks measured them in 1985, one trunk was 19 inches across and the other 26.4. The register gives a height of about 18.7 metres. Those measurements are forty years old now, and nobody has published newer ones, so if you bring a tape, tell us what you find. What these trees have witnessed is mostly the quiet business of a cemetery. More than a century of visitors walking between the stones, and a husband's memorial that kept growing long after the planting. A recent observation records the beeches still standing. The cemetery is open to visitors, but check maplegrovecemetery.org for hours before you go. Our pin is approximate, placed by the register inside the grounds, so look for the Riis grave and the two trunks beside it.

trees.name: The White Oak of Woodlawn

location.address: Woodlawn Cemetery, North Border Ave and Rutgers Ave, overlooking East 233rd Street

trees.story: When New York drew up its first list of Great Trees in 1985, NYC Parks called this white oak the oldest tree in Woodlawn Cemetery. It is still one of the largest. The city measured its trunk at 64.2 inches across, a little over five metres round, with a height of about 27 metres and a crown 82 feet wide. Woodlawn's own arboretum page describes a massive white oak guarding the north edge of the cemetery, and counts it among 33 trees on the grounds with trunks five feet across or more. It stands at North Border and Rutgers Avenues, looking out over East 233rd Street. The title of oldest is no longer settled. In 2024 Parks added a black oak in Woodlawn's northeast corner and estimated it at nearly 300 years, without saying how the two compare. Nobody has published an age for this white oak at all, so the two claims sit side by side, one a ranking and one a number. If you know the history of either, tell us. The cemetery is free to walk in and open daily from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM, and its trees carry trunk labels and appear on the Woodlawn tree walk map. Our pin uses the Parks coordinate and is approximate at cemetery scale, so use the map and the label to find the trunk.

trees.name: The Weeping Beech of the Gould Plot

location.address: Woodlawn Cemetery, Jay Gould plot near the Gould Mausoleum

trees.story: The Gould family built a mausoleum at Woodlawn, and the tree beside it has done a better job of looking permanent. This European weeping beech stands on the Jay Gould plot, near the Gould Mausoleum, and NYC Parks has listed it as a Great Tree since 1985. Parks describes twisting branches over a smooth, leathery trunk, and a canopy 63.5 feet across. Woodlawn lists a weeping European beech among the 33 trees on its grounds with trunks five feet across or more, which tells you the scale to expect. Its exact size is a small mystery. The Parks register carries the same figure, 53.3, in both its diameter and height columns, a copying slip that leaves neither number trustworthy. Nobody has published when it was planted either. The age of the mausoleum is not the age of the tree, and no source ties the two, so its age stays open. If you know, tell us. The cemetery is free to enter and open daily from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM. Its trees carry trunk labels and are mapped on the Woodlawn tree walk, which is the surest way to find this one, since our pin is the Parks coordinate and only approximate. Come in autumn, when the hanging curtain of leaves turns gold and copper.

trees.name: The Cutleaf Beech of the Woodbine Plot

location.address: Woodlawn Cemetery, Woodbine Plot, northeast of the Jerome Avenue entrance

trees.story: At about 28 metres, this beech stands as tall as a nine-storey building, and its leaves look nothing like a beech's should. It is a cutleaf European beech, the unusual fine-leaved form that Woodlawn's arboretum page singles out among the 33 trees on its grounds with trunks five feet across or more. NYC Parks made it a Great Tree in 1985 and records it at 91 feet tall with a crown 50.5 feet wide. Parks offers a neat comparison. The bark is like that of the cemetery's weeping beeches, but the tree stands upright, without their drooping form. So you get the bark of a beech and a tall, conventional crown, and only when you look up at the leaves does the oddity show. It stands in the Woodbine Plot, northeast of the Jerome Avenue entrance, which makes it one of the first Great Trees you can reach after stepping off the 4 train at Woodlawn. One number on the register is best ignored. It gives a trunk diameter of 91.2 inches, which simply echoes the height figure in the next column. Nobody has published a planting date or an age. If you know when the Woodbine Plot was planted, or this tree's history, tell us. The cemetery is free and open daily from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM, and its trees are labelled on the trunk and mapped on the Woodlawn tree walk. Our pin is approximate, from the Parks coordinate.

trees.name: The White Pine by the Jerome Avenue Gate

location.address: Woodlawn Cemetery near the Jerome Avenue entrance

trees.story: NYC Parks describes this tree with an honesty that registers rarely allow themselves. It calls its shape scraggly and twisted, the look of an old white pine, and then lists it as a Great Tree anyway, as it has since 1985. That is the case for it in one line. Woodlawn's own arboretum page names a native eastern white pine among its Great Trees, a local species holding its own among the European beeches and the Japanese umbrella pine on the same list. Its crown spreads about 48 feet. It is also the easiest of Woodlawn's listed trees to find. It stands near the Jerome Avenue entrance, the gate right beside the 4 train's last stop at Woodlawn, so you can see a Great Tree within a few minutes of leaving the platform. Beyond the crown, the record goes quiet. The Parks register puts the same number, 83.64, in both its diameter and its height columns, which cannot both be right, so neither is a measurement we can repeat. Nobody has published an age either, so old is the register's word and the only one we have. If you know its history, tell us. The grounds are free to walk in and open daily from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM. Trees carry trunk labels and appear on the Woodlawn tree walk. Our pin, from the Parks coordinate, is approximate.

trees.name: The Umbrella Pine of Woodlawn

location.address: Woodlawn Cemetery, corner of Parkview and Chestnut Avenues, northeast of the Paterno mausoleum

trees.story: A conifer from Japan has been one of New York's official Great Trees for forty years, at a cemetery crossroads in the Bronx. This Japanese umbrella pine stands at the corner of Parkview and Chestnut Avenues in Woodlawn Cemetery, northeast of the Paterno mausoleum, and NYC Parks has listed it since 1985. Parks calls it a unique conifer native to Japan, and records a crown only 22.5 feet across. Beside the 82-foot spread of Woodlawn's great white oak, that is modest. Size was never its argument. Woodlawn's own arboretum page names it among the cemetery's Great Trees, alongside native oaks and a white pine, as one of the plants that make these grounds an arboretum as much as a burial ground. The umbrella of the common name describes its needles, which radiate in whorls like the ribs of an opened umbrella, the single detail that makes it easy to pick out once you are at the right corner. Its other numbers are missing. The Parks register carries the same figure, 47.56, in both its diameter and height columns, a copying slip, so neither can be trusted. No planting date or age has been published. If you know when it went in, tell us. The cemetery is free and open daily from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM, trees carry trunk labels, and the Woodlawn tree walk map shows where they stand. Our pin, from the Parks coordinate, is approximate.

trees.name: The Black Oak of Woodlawn's Northeast Corner

location.address: Woodlawn Cemetery, northeast corner

trees.story: This oak was already old when Woodlawn Cemetery was laid out around it, and the planners decided to keep it. NYC Parks says the black oak in the cemetery's northeast corner was recognised as exceptional and preserved when the grounds were first designed, and it estimates the tree at nearly 300 years old. Parks does not say what that estimate rests on, so take it as the city's best judgement rather than a count of rings. If it holds, the tree started growing in the early 1700s, when New York was still a British colony. Woodlawn's arboretum page puts the trunk at six feet across, close to six metres round, and Parks calls it absolutely massive. It only joined the city's list of Great Trees in 2024, almost forty years after the first list named a white oak on the north edge of these same grounds as the oldest tree in Woodlawn. The two claims have never been reconciled. One is a ranking from 1985 with no age attached, the other an estimate from 2024 with no comparison. They stand about 330 metres apart, so you can judge both. If you know anything firmer about either tree's age, tell us. The cemetery is free to enter and open daily from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM. Trees carry trunk labels and are mapped on the Woodlawn tree walk, which is the way to find this one; our pin, from the Parks coordinate, is approximate.

trees.name: The Linden of Duke Ellington's Jazz Corner

location.address: Woodlawn Cemetery, Jazz Corner, overlooking the Duke Ellington family lot

trees.story: Duke Ellington chose his grave for a tree. In 1959 he bought a family lot at Woodlawn Cemetery, drawn, NYC Parks says, by a stately linden, and he sketched the tree into his own plans for the memorial. The tree is a small-leaved lime, the species Americans call littleleaf linden, and it has become the centre of the cemetery's Jazz Corner. Around it are the memorials of Miles Davis, Lionel Hampton, Max Roach, Illinois Jacquet, Clark Terry and Coleman Hawkins. Few trees in New York keep company like that. Parks added it to the Great Trees list in 2024, and for once the reason on the register is not size. Parks gives no trunk measurement, height or age, and nobody else has published one, so we cannot tell you how big it is or how long it had stood before Ellington found it. If you know, tell us. What the record does say is that the tree came first. Ellington picked the spot because of it, and the corner grew around them both. Woodlawn Cemetery is free to walk in and open daily from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM. Its trees carry trunk labels and are mapped on the Woodlawn tree walk, and the Ellington lot is the landmark to look for, since our pin is the Parks coordinate and approximate at cemetery scale. Come in early summer, when the linden flowers.

trees.name: The Japanese Maple of Woodlawn

location.address: Woodlawn Cemetery, between Central Avenue and Spruce Avenue

trees.story: Woodlawn Cemetery holds more than 300 old Japanese maples, and this one was chosen to speak for all of them. When NYC Parks added it to the Great Trees list in 2024, it named this tree as the representative of that whole population, planted across the cemetery in the 1900s. The detail Parks gives about how they got this way is the best part. The gardeners who planted them learned not to prune them. Parks describes this one as gnarled and sculptural, and it was picked to show what Woodlawn's maples have become. It is not even, strictly, a single tree. Parks says it was planted as a group of four. It stands between Central Avenue and Spruce Avenue in the cemetery. There is no measurement on the register, no height and no trunk size, and no planting year more exact than the 1900s, so its age is open. If you know when this group went in, tell us. A maple chosen out of three hundred deserves a slow look. Walk round it before you walk on, since a sculptural tree changes shape with every step. Woodlawn is free to enter and open daily from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM. Its trees carry trunk labels and appear on the Woodlawn tree walk map, the surest way to find this one; our pin is the Parks coordinate and approximate at cemetery scale.

trees.name: The American Elm of Wave Hill

location.address: Wave Hill, 4900 Independence Avenue, top of the lawn southeast of Wave Hill House

trees.story: This elm stands about 35 metres tall, and in the 2000s it caught Dutch elm disease and lived. NYC Parks recorded it at 114.8 feet, with a trunk 57.1 inches across, a little over four and a half metres round, when it put the tree on its first list of Great Trees in 1985. It grows at the top of the lawn southeast of Wave Hill House in Riverdale, and Parks gives a precise tip for seeing it. Stand under the arbor of the Shade Border, where its vase-like shape shows best. Nobody knows quite how it got here. Wave Hill estimates it began growing in the early to mid-1800s, somewhere around two centuries ago, and says it may have been planted by the estate's owners or may simply have come up on its own. Those are two different stories for the same tree, and the garden has not chosen between them. Parks counts it a survivor of the disease. It does not stand alone. The same lawn holds a sugar maple that Parks puts close to 200 years and a lacebark pine that Wave Hill says went in in the early 1900s, both Great Trees too. Wave Hill is a public garden with paid entry, open Tuesday to Sunday, with free Thursdays; check wavehill.org for current hours. Our pin is the lawn coordinate Parks gives for all three, so it is approximate.

trees.name: The White Ash of the Bedford Park Gate

location.address: New York Botanical Garden, near the Bedford Park Boulevard entrance, overlooking Conservatory Drive

trees.story: NYC Parks calls this tree a rare survivor of the emerald ash borer, and it stands by one of the gates of the New York Botanical Garden. It is a white ash at least 100 feet tall, with a trunk 47 inches across, about three and three-quarter metres round, and in 2024 the city added it to its list of Great Trees. It stands near the Bedford Park Boulevard entrance, overlooking Conservatory Drive. Its origin comes with a small puzzle. Parks describes it as a remnant of old New York hardwood forest. In the same entry it cites the garden's records, which say the tree was donated in 1907 by John Finley, the Foreman of the Gardeners. A donated tree and a forest remnant are hard to square, and the records do not say whether it was planted that year or arrived already grown. If the 1907 gift is the tree's start, it is about 120 years old. If it is older forest stock, it could be more. We give the gift date as the best documented figure and leave the rest open. If you know more of the Finley story, tell us. The garden is ticketed, so check nybg.org for hours and prices before you go. Our pin is the Parks coordinate and approximate, so head for the Bedford Park Boulevard gate and look up.

trees.name: The Sycamore of the Everett Garden Gate

location.address: New York Botanical Garden, just northeast of the Everett Garden Gate

trees.story: Nobody planted this sycamore. NYC Parks says it seeded itself on the grounds of the New York Botanical Garden, so in a garden of chosen specimens, this one chose itself. It stands just northeast of the Everett Garden Gate, and its huge branches, Parks notes, shade the school groups that gather there. It has been measured at least twice. A site-wide tree survey by the WPA, the Depression-era public works programme, recorded the trunk at 46 inches across. When the city added the tree to its Great Trees list in 2024, it was 57 inches, about four and a half metres round. Eleven inches of trunk is the visible record of the decades between the two visits. What the survey said beyond that number is lost to us, since the sentence on the Parks page breaks off. We do not know when the tree came up, only that it was already big enough to log when the WPA crews came through, so its age is an open question. If the garden's archive dates it, tell us. The garden is ticketed, so check nybg.org for hours and prices. Our pin is the Parks coordinate and approximate. Look for the biggest spreading tree beside the Everett Garden Gate.

trees.name: The Oak of U Thant's Forest Walk

location.address: Raoul Wallenberg Forest, off the Palisades Avenue hiking trail

trees.story: The directions to this oak use a dead tree as a signpost. NYC Parks tells you to leave Palisades Avenue on the trail a tenth of a mile north of West 232nd Street, climb about 500 feet to the trunk of a dead copper beech, then go 200 feet southeast. There, in the Raoul Wallenberg Forest in Riverdale, stands a white oak that has been one of New York's Great Trees since the first list in 1985. Parks associates it with U Thant, the Burmese diplomat who was Secretary General of the United Nations from 1961 to 1971 and lived in Riverdale. The register does not say what the connection was, and we will not guess. If you know the story, tell us. The tree itself is big. Its trunk is 57 inches across, about four and a half metres round, and Parks puts it at 87.7 feet tall, about 27 metres. Nobody has published an age. Go soon, and go gently. The city's forestry inventory, which carries the same coordinates as the Parks listing, last recorded it in September 2023 and rated its condition poor. It was alive then, but that is the last word we have. The trail is a real hiking path, uneven underfoot, and entry to the forest is free. Our pin comes from the register's own tree record, so once you have found the dead beech, the oak is close.

trees.name: The Green Ash of Crotona Park

location.address: Crotona Park, south of the Prospect Avenue entrance, behind the playground

trees.story: This tree is on a medication schedule. NYC Parks treats the green ash behind the Crotona Park playground at regular intervals against the emerald ash borer, an insect that attacks ash trees, and so far the tree is holding up. When the city's forestry inventory last checked it, in September 2026, it rated its condition good. In 2024 Parks added it to its list of Great Trees and described its commanding presence on the path. The trunk is 55 inches across, about four and a third metres round. It stands south of the Prospect Avenue entrance, on the path between the soccer field and the playground, which gives one of the city's official Great Trees about as ordinary an address as a tree can have. Nobody has published when it was planted or how old it is, and we will not pick a number without a source. If you know its history, or remember it from decades of games on that field, tell us. Crotona Park has a second Great Tree, an American elm near the Claremont Parkway entrance, about 550 metres away, so the two make a short Bronx circuit, and both are free to visit. Our pin comes from the forestry inventory's own record of this tree, matched to the Parks listing, so it is confirmed.

trees.name: The Mazzard Cherry of Ewen Park

location.address: Ewen Park, mid-park just south of the dog run

trees.story: One of the largest and oldest trees in Ewen Park is a cherry. NYC Parks says so in the entry that put this mazzard, the wild sweet cherry, on its list of Great Trees in 2024, and it is the kind of sentence that makes you look twice at a tree most people would pass for an ordinary flowering one. The trunk is 28 inches across, a little over two metres round, and Parks notes that it flowers in spring. It stands mid-park in Riverdale, just south of the dog run, so the likeliest company you will have while looking at it is somebody's dog. The city's forestry inventory last checked it in April 2025 and rated it in good condition, with coordinates that match the Parks listing exactly. Our pin comes from that record and is confirmed, which in a park full of trees is worth having. What nobody has written down is its age. Parks calls it one of the park's oldest without putting a number to it, and there is no planting date on record, so how long it has been flowering here is an open question. If you know, or have photographs of it from years back, tell us. The park is free and open to all, and the usual approach is from the 1 train at 231st Street. Come in spring if you can, when the cherry is in flower and the Great Tree label suddenly makes sense.
