trees.name: The Willow Oak of Herbert Street

location.address: In front of 86 Herbert Street

trees.story: In East Williamsburg, the biggest tree you can see for many blocks stands on the sidewalk in front of 86 Herbert Street. That is how NYC Parks describes it, and the people who live around it said so first. This willow oak became a Great Tree in 2024 after the community nominated it, the most direct way a tree can join the list. Somebody who passed it every day decided it deserved the city's attention, and the city agreed. Its trunk is 39 inches across, about three metres round, on an ordinary residential block. A willow oak is an oak that does not look like one. Its leaves are long and narrow, like a willow's, so from a distance this one could pass for the wrong tree entirely, and only the acorns give the family away. The city's forestry inventory last checked it in January 2026 and rated its condition fair, alive and holding. The coordinates on that record match the Parks listing, so our pin is confirmed. Nobody has published its age or planting date, and we will not guess one from the size. If you know when it went in, or remember the street before it was this big, tell us. It is a street tree on a public sidewalk, so it is free and always there. Stand across the street to take in the crown, and leave the front steps to the people who live behind it.

trees.name: The Shumard Oak of Sixth Avenue

location.address: 385 6th Avenue

trees.story: Park Slope has changed around this oak, and the oak has stayed put. When NYC Parks named it a Great Tree in 2024, that was the reason it gave. The Shumard oak in front of 385 6th Avenue was chosen for standing the test of time while the neighbourhood transformed around it. It is a street tree, on a public sidewalk, with a trunk 47 inches across by the Parks listing and 48 by the city's forestry inventory, close to three and three-quarter metres round either way. The inch between the two is the sort of gap you get from two surveys at different times, not a dispute. Parks describes the Shumard as a fast-growing oak, which is worth keeping in mind before reading an age into that trunk. A fast grower reaches this size sooner than a slow one, so the girth does not translate neatly into years, and nobody has published a planting date. Its age stays open. If you know when it went in, tell us. What you can plan around is the colour. Parks notes that its leaves turn red to orange in autumn, which on a city street is the kind of thing people stop for. The forestry inventory last checked it in November 2025 and rated it in good condition, with coordinates matching the Parks listing, so our pin is confirmed. It is free and always there. Come in autumn, and look up from the sidewalk rather than the stoop.

trees.name: The Umbrella Elm of West 1st Street

location.address: Near 1769 West 1st Street

trees.story: This American elm in Gravesend made New York's list of Great Trees for its shape. NYC Parks says it was selected in 2024 as a splendid tree with impressive form, and describes its crown as a nearly perfectly full umbrella. Not age, not fame, not a story. Just a street tree that grew into the outline a child would draw. The trunk is 51 inches across, a little over four metres round, which would be enough to notice it even without the shape. It stands on the public sidewalk near 1769 West 1st Street. The city's forestry inventory last checked it in February 2026, rated its condition good, and placed it at the same coordinates as the Parks listing, so our pin is confirmed. Nobody has published when it was planted or how old it is, so we leave the number blank. If you know the tree's history, or have an old photograph of the street with it in, tell us. Because the shape is the point, distance helps. Cross the street, or stand a few houses down, and the umbrella comes into focus in a way it never does from directly underneath. It is free, on a public sidewalk, and always there.

trees.name: The Elm of 55th Avenue

location.address: 92-22 55th Avenue

trees.story: There is an American elm in Elmhurst that stands taller than the houses on its street. NYC Parks says it towers above them, with a large spreading canopy, and in 2024 the city made it a Great Tree. The neighbourhood's name and the tree's species are a pleasing match, though no source we know of says the one has anything to do with the other, so enjoy the coincidence and leave it there. The trunk has two measurements that differ a little. The Parks listing gives 51 inches across. The city's forestry inventory, checked in June 2026, gives 54. That works out at somewhere around four metres round, and the three-inch gap is the ordinary result of different surveys at different times, not a quarrel about the tree. The inventory rated it in good condition, alive and well on a Queens sidewalk, and its coordinates match the Parks listing, so our pin is confirmed. It stands in front of 92-22 55th Avenue. Nobody has published its age or a planting date. If you know when it went in, or how the street looked before it outgrew the roofs, tell us. Because it is a street tree, it is free and always there, but the people behind it live there too. The best view of a canopy that tops the houses is from across the street or a little way down the block, where you can see how much sky it takes up.

trees.name: The Willow Oak of Perry Avenue

location.address: 3331 Perry Avenue

trees.story: This oak grew a trunk 55 inches across in a strip of ground that NYC Parks itself calls narrow and congested. That was the case for nominating it. When the willow oak in front of 3331 Perry Avenue in Norwood became a Great Tree in 2024, Parks said it was put forward for its size despite its growing conditions, which is the official way of saying it had no business getting this big where it is. Fifty-five inches across is about four and a half metres round. For comparison, the Herbert Street willow oak in Brooklyn, another Great Tree of the same species chosen the same year, is 39 inches. This one is the larger by a wide margin. The city's forestry inventory last checked it in April 2025, rated its condition good, and gives coordinates that match the Parks listing, so our pin is confirmed. Willow oaks carry narrow, willow-shaped leaves rather than the lobed ones most people picture on an oak, so look for the size first and the leaves second. Nobody has published its age or when it was planted. If you know, or have lived on Perry Avenue long enough to remember it smaller, tell us. It is a street tree on a public sidewalk, free and always there.

trees.name: The Weeping Beech of Cypress Hills National Cemetery

location.address: Cypress Hills National Cemetery, 625 Jamaica Avenue, north of Norwood Avenue at Jamaica Avenue

trees.story: This weeping beech spreads over a burial ground of more than 21,000 veterans and their dependents, 24 of them holders of the Medal of Honor. NYC Parks describes the beech at Cypress Hills National Cemetery as far-reaching, hovering over those graves, and in 2024 it made the tree a Great Tree. Cypress Hills is, by the Parks account, the only national cemetery in New York City, which gives a single tree here an unusual charge. It is a European weeping beech, a cultivated form whose branches hang rather than reach, planted in a place built for remembering. The register gives no measurements, no trunk size, no height and no age, and nobody else has published them, so the story here is the setting rather than the numbers. If you know when the beech was planted, or have measured it, tell us. Visiting needs a little care. The cemetery is free and open to visitors, and the Department of Veterans Affairs has listed it as open daily from 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM, but that listing comes from an older copy of its page, so confirm the hours before you go. It is a working national cemetery, and the people at the graves may be there for their own family. Our pin is the Parks coordinate and approximate at cemetery scale, north of Norwood Avenue at Jamaica Avenue. Come in autumn, when the hanging curtain of leaves turns gold and copper over the stones.

trees.name: Willow Oak of Herbert Street

location.address: 86 Herbert Street, East Williamsburg, Brooklyn (street tree on the sidewalk)

trees.story:
Most of the Great Trees of New York City stand in parks and cemeteries. This willow oak stands on the sidewalk in front of 86 Herbert Street, in East Williamsburg, and in 2024 NYC Parks added it to the list in an update that brought 17 Brooklyn trees on board.

The city's street tree census counted it in 2015 at 34 inches across at chest height, about 2.7 metres around the trunk, alive and in good health. It is the only willow oak recorded at that address.

Willow oak is a southern species, native across the south-eastern United States. It takes its name from its leaves, which are long and narrow like a willow's rather than lobed like those of the northern oaks, so it looks unlike the oaks most New Yorkers know.

No source we found gives the year it was planted, so this page gives no age. One press report calls it a weeping oak, while the census and the Parks list both say willow oak.

You can see all of it from the public pavement, and nothing is needed to get in.
